title: Chronos: event-driven runbook scheduler for operator tasks
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: our current runbooks are either manual or encoded as monolithic scripts with poor visibility and brittle concurrency controls. Operators spend time coordinating handoffs and throttling external rate-limited APIs during incident responses.

Goal: build Chronos, a lightweight, event-driven runbook scheduler that converts textual runbooks into executable task DAGs with safe concurrency, rate limits, retries, and first-class dry-run/preview. Provide a small CLI plugin surface for admin utilities and a sandboxed web UI for operators to run/preview playbooks. Integrate with RBAC, audit logs, and the Console's tracing so every run is observable and auditable.

Out of scope for this ticket: full on-call workflow integration, long-term downstream analytics (will be a follow-up). The initial launch targets internal SRE/Support teams only.
acceptance_criteria: Chronos service can ingest a YAML/Markdown runbook and compile it into an executable DAG within the sandbox environment
Operators can execute a runbook in dry-run mode and receive a deterministic preview of steps and resource effects
Per-step rate limiting and concurrency locks are enforced (configurable per-runbook) and verified in integration tests
CLI plugin (chronosctl) exposes runbook upload, list, dry-run, trigger, and status; CLI passes basic acceptance tests
All executions emit structured telemetry (trace id, step latencies, success/failure) and appear in Console with per-run metrics
RBAC gates runbook execution via existing org/team roles; audit logs capture start/stop/override events
notes_or_design_decisions: Architecture: lightweight scheduler + worker pool. Scheduler compiles runbook to DAG and stores in Postgres (compact), workers pick up tasks from a prioritized queue (Redis streams) to preserve ordering and provide backpressure.

Why not use existing Airflow/Kubernetes Job semantics: those systems are heavyweight for short-lived operator tasks and add cognitive overhead during incidents. Chronos prioritizes sub-second scheduling and integrated CLI ergonomics.
Locking: use a Redis-based distributed lock per resource key (e.g., external API token) to avoid concurrent steps that could exceed quotas. Fallback policy configured to queue vs. fail fast.
Safety: every destructive step must include an explicit confirmation token in the runbook; the runner will require a confirm flag or a signed approval when run remotely.
Observability trade-off: choose structured events (JSON) over verbose logs for faster index and query in the Console; initial retention 30 days (configurable).
